newsitem.title: ALBANIA: New EU mission visits chaotic Albania for aid talks.
newsitem.headline: New EU mission visits chaotic Albania for aid talks.

text.p: A new European Union mission visits Albania on Wednesday to work out how to help the anarchic Balkan state, as some countries consider sending troops to protect relief missions.

The 10-member EU delegation, the second in two weeks after an indecisive first visit, hoped to meet Prime Minister Bashkim Fino to discuss the armed unrest sweeping the former communist country, in which more than 100 people have died.

A Dutch reporter was in hospital on the nearby Greek island of Corfu after she was shot in the Albanian port town of Sarande on Tuesday, the first foreign correspondent to suffer serious injury in the violence.
Colleagues said Wilma Goudappel, a freelance reporter, was apparently targeted by a sniper outside her villa. She was in a serious condition but expected to recover.

Albania has repeatedly called for a multinational force to help it restore order, but EU foreign ministers have shied away from backing full-scale military intervention while saying that its member states can act independently.

Italy said on Tuesday that military experts from six countries had already flown to Albania for talks on the possible deployment of a multinational protection force as part of the EU relief mission to Europe's poorest state.

Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta said the team comprised representatives of the four countries that make up the Florence-based Eurofor force -- conceived by France, Italy, Portugal and Spain for peacekeeping and relief operations -- as well as generals from Greece and Austria.
Non-EU members Turkey and Romania have said they are willing to join such a force. The EU estimates that Albania urgently needs some $10 million of basic medical supplies and 10,000 tonnes of flour.

Much of the south of the country is in the hands of heavily-armed gangs who are demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha after hundreds of thousands of Albanians lost cash in the collapse of popular savings schemes.

In the port of Durres, a group of would-be emigrants tried to get two rusted-up dredgers to work, hoping to reach Italy along with thousands who crammed onto barely-seaworthy vessels ranging from fishing boats to freighters.
But when the communist-era dredgers failed to work, they set fire to them in disgust.
Sporadic gunfire rattled around the capital early on Wednesday, with armoured vehicles patrolling the streets during an overnight curfew.
Police in the capital have been issued with bullet-proof vests, even for traffic duty, but most shops and businesses are opening normally in the daytime.
Trying to calm worries about the unrest, Defence Minister Shaqir Vukaj told a visiting American admiral on Tuesday the government remained in full control of heavy weapons and the air force.

Albanian television also reported that some police stations had successfuly recovered arms looted from military depots. It said 1.2 million bullets had been recovered by one police station in the capital.
On Wednesday, parliament was to debate the terms of a possible amnesty for prisoners freed from jail during the rioting across the country.
